title: Paradise Lost
author: John Milton
written: Composed largely in the 1650s and early 1660s, by dictation
setting: Hell, Chaos, Heaven and the garden of Eden, in the days around the Fall
lengthNote: Over ten thousand lines of unrhymed iambic pentameter, arranged in twelve books
openingLine: Of Man’s first disobedience, and the fruit Of that forbidden Tree, whose mortal taste Brought death into the world, and all our woe
summary: A blind republican, on the losing side of a revolution, writes an epic about the first defeat. Milton gives the rebel angel the best speeches and then spends twelve books showing what those speeches lead to, and the crisis of the poem is a conversation between a husband and a wife about whether to work apart for a morning. It ends with two people walking into an unmapped world, holding hands.
referenceStyle: book — the source text carries no line numbers, so quotations are placed by book alone

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Paradise Lost
sourceText.note: The text used for checking runs one verse line to a line but prints no line numbers, so references here stop at the book. Line numbers in printed editions follow the twelve-book arrangement of 1674.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: In ten books, from a London still rebuilding after the Fire.

atAGlance.label: Second edition
atAGlance.note: Books VII and X were each divided in two, giving the twelve books now standard, and the year Milton died.

atAGlance.label: Verse
atAGlance.note: Milton added a note defending the absence of rhyme, which he called no necessary adjunct of a poem.

atAGlance.label: Composition
atAGlance.note: Milton had been entirely blind since about 1652; the poem was spoken to whoever was at hand to write.

structure.label: Book I
structure.title: The fallen angels, and Pandemonium
structure.summary: The fallen angels come to on a burning lake, and Satan makes the worst news imaginable into a programme. The roll-call of the devils doubles as a catalogue of the gods later worshipped on earth, and Pandemonium rises out of the ground in the time it takes to describe it.

structure.label: Book II
structure.title: The debate, the gates, and the flight through Chaos
structure.summary: Hell holds a policy meeting with four speakers and a fixed outcome, since Beelzebub is arguing Satan's case for him. Satan then leaves alone, meets his own daughter and grandson keeping the gate, and beats his way up through Chaos towards the new world.

structure.label: Book III
structure.title: God foresees the Fall, and the Son offers himself
structure.summary: God sees Satan coming and states, in advance, that man will fall and that the fall will be man's own doing. The Son volunteers to pay for it. The book opens with the poem's most personal passage, an address to light by a man who cannot see it.

structure.label: Book IV
structure.title: Satan in Eden
structure.summary: Satan reaches the garden and finds that he has brought Hell with him. What follows is mostly domestic: two people gardening, talking, going to bed, while the intruder squats beside them taking notes and the angelic guard finally moves him on.

structure.label: Book V
structure.title: Raphael’s visit, and Abdiel
structure.summary: Eve wakes from a dream she did not choose, and Raphael arrives to eat fruit and explain the terms. His history of the revolt gives the poem Abdiel, the one angel who hears Satan's argument through and walks out of the meeting.

structure.label: Book VI
structure.title: The war in Heaven
structure.summary: Angels fight, invent artillery, throw hills at each other and cannot be killed, which is precisely the point: the war is unwinnable until the Son ends it alone in a single afternoon. Force is shown to be the least interesting power in the poem.

structure.label: Book VII
structure.title: The Creation
structure.summary: Raphael answers Adam's question about how the world began. Milton's six days are noisy, crowded and physical, full of animals shouldering their way out of the ground, and the whole account is framed as speech accommodated to a listener who could not otherwise follow it.

structure.label: Book VIII
structure.title: Adam’s story, and Raphael’s warning
structure.summary: Adam asks about astronomy and is told to be lowly wise. He then describes his first minutes of consciousness, his argument with God about loneliness, and his response to Eve — at which Raphael frowns and delivers the poem's least comfortable piece of marital advice.

structure.label: Book IX
structure.title: The separation, and the Fall
structure.summary: The crisis is a disagreement about how to spend a working day. Eve wants a virtue that has been tested; Adam gives way sooner than command her; the serpent finds her alone and argues her into eating, and Adam eats knowing exactly what he is doing. The book ends in mutual accusation.

structure.label: Book X
structure.title: Judgement, and the road built from Hell
structure.summary: The Son comes down to sentence them and stays to clothe them. Sin and Death pave a highway from Hell to earth, Satan returns to an ovation that turns into hissing, and Eve — who is blamed for everything — is the first to propose that they stop blaming each other.

structure.label: Book XI
structure.title: Michael’s visions of the future
structure.summary: Michael takes Adam up a hill and shows him what his choice has produced: the first murder, a lazar-house of diseases, war, and a flood. Adam learns history the way a man learns of a bereavement, one instance at a time.

structure.label: Book XII
structure.title: Michael’s narration, and leaving Eden
structure.summary: Michael switches from vision to narration and carries the story to the Incarnation and beyond. Adam is offered a paradise that cannot be lost because it is internal, and the poem closes on two figures walking away with the whole world to choose from.

characters.name: Satan
characters.role: Leader of the rebel angels, formerly Lucifer
characters.summary: The most persuasive speaker in English poetry and the one the poem most wants you to distrust. He is magnificent in Books I and II, cannot stop talking to himself in Book IV, and by Book IX has agreed to be squeezed into a snake — a career the poem records as a steady shrinking.
characters.clue: He calls the worst place in creation his own possession, decides that his mind can furnish it, and ends the poem in the body of an animal.

characters.name: Eve
characters.summary: She is given the poem's best argument — that an untested virtue is not virtue at all — and the poem never answers it, only shows what happens next. She also speaks its tenderest lines and makes the first move towards reconciliation after the Fall, while Adam is still composing his complaint.
characters.clue: She proposes that they work apart for one morning, wins the argument, and the world changes before lunch.

characters.name: Adam
characters.summary: An archangel tells him the whole truth in advance and he falls anyway, because he will not live without her; ignorance has nothing to do with it. Milton is careful about this: Adam is not deceived, which makes his eating the more deliberate act and the harder one to condemn cleanly.
characters.clue: Warned in person, at length, by an angel over dinner, he still swallows the fruit within seconds of learning what she has done.

characters.name: God the Father
characters.summary: Milton puts him on the stand in Book III and has him argue his own case: the angels and man were made free, freedom that cannot fail is not freedom, and therefore the blame is not his. Readers have found the voice cold ever since, which may be the price of making an argument instead of an atmosphere.

characters.name: The Son
characters.role: The Father's agent in war, creation, judgement and mercy
characters.summary: He does everything in the poem that actually takes effect: he ends the war alone, speaks the world into being, passes sentence in Eden and then kneels down to clothe the people he has sentenced. Where Satan announces, the Son acts and says very little about it.

characters.name: Raphael
characters.role: The affable archangel, sent to warn Adam
characters.summary: He comes to lunch and stays for four books, explaining the revolt, the war and the creation in terms a person without experience of either could hold. His honesty has limits he admits to, and his parting advice — be lowly wise — is the one instruction Adam and Eve both fail to keep.
traits: candid about what he cannot say

characters.name: Michael
characters.role: The archangel who carries out the eviction
characters.summary: He leads the loyal host in the war and returns in the last two books as the poem's historian, showing Adam the future in pictures until the pictures become unbearable and he switches to plain narration. He is the one who names the paradise within.

characters.name: Abdiel
characters.role: A seraph among the rebel legions
characters.summary: Milton invents him. He hears out Satan's case for independence, answers it in public, and then walks the whole night back through an army that despises him. For a poet who had defended a beheaded king's executioners and then watched the monarchy return, the figure of the lone dissenter was not an abstraction.
characters.clue: One angel out of an entire rebel legion says no, argues the point, and walks out alone through a jeering camp.

characters.name: Beelzebub
characters.role: Satan's second, and the voice of the winning motion
characters.summary: He speaks last in the debate in Hell and proposes the plan Satan wants, which the assembly then adopts as its own idea. The manoeuvre is the most recognisable piece of politics in the poem: the leader does not have to argue for his policy if the right subordinate does.

characters.name: Sin and Death
characters.summary: Half allegory and half family, they are Satan's daughter and his son by her, and they guard the door he needs opened. Once the Fall has happened they build a bridge from Hell to earth, and a moral idea becomes a piece of civil engineering.

themes.name: Freedom, foreknowledge and fault
themes.summary: The poem’s stated purpose is to justify the ways of God to men, and its argument is all about liberty: obedience that could not have been withheld would prove nothing, so the possibility of the Fall is the price of everything good in Eden. God knows what will happen and insists this is not the same as causing it.
themes.development: Set out as doctrine in Book III, dramatised as a marital argument in Book IX, and left with Adam in Book XII as a choice about how to live in a world where the worst has already happened.

themes.name: Persuasion
themes.summary: Almost every turn of the plot is a speech that works. Satan raises an army with one, carries a parliament with another through a proxy, and takes Eden with a third; the loyal side answers with Abdiel's rebuttal and Raphael's patient exposition. Milton, who wrote pamphlets for a revolution, knew how much damage a good argument can do.
themes.development: From public oratory in Books I and II, to private flattery in Book IX, to the quieter persuasion of Michael's history, which changes Adam without once raising its voice.

themes.name: Rule and service
themes.summary: Satan frames the whole conflict as a choice between reigning and serving, and the poem spends twelve books dismantling the opposition. Service in Heaven turns out to be a form of activity and delight; Satan's reign is a monarchy of one over a wasteland, maintained by speeches to people who have no alternative.
themes.development: Announced in Book I as a preference, tested in the Hell debate, and answered in Book VI, where the Son's single-handed victory shows what authority looks like when it does not need to be asserted.

themes.name: Manhood and gender
themes.summary: The poem states a hierarchy plainly and then writes scenes that strain against it. Eve is described as made for Adam, and it is Eve who produces the argument nobody refutes, who eats first, and who ends the quarrel after the Fall. Milton’s hierarchy is doctrine; his drama keeps handing the initiative to the wrong person.
themes.development: Declared in Book IV, accepted by Eve in her own voice, contested in the separation scene of Book IX, and reversed without comment at the end of Book X.

themes.name: Knowledge and its limits
themes.summary: The forbidden tree is a tree of knowledge, and the poem is full of people asking questions they are told not to press: Adam on astronomy, Eve on what the fruit might do, Satan on whether he was created at all. Raphael’s answer is that some knowledge is no use to the person who wants it; he does not call curiosity wicked.
themes.development: Raphael’s warning in Book VIII comes back in the serpent’s temptation as its exact opposite, knowledge offered as promotion, and is settled in Book XII, where what Adam needs turns out to be practice, not information.

themes.name: Loss and exile
themes.summary: Everyone in the poem has been thrown out of somewhere. The angels lose Heaven, Adam and Eve lose the garden, and Milton — blind, out of favour, on the wrong side of a restored monarchy — writes the loss from the inside. What the ending offers is a version of paradise they can carry with them.
themes.development: Hell in Book I is exile as rage; Book IV is exile as homesickness watching other people's happiness; Book XII makes it a journey with a direction, undertaken hand in hand.

techniques.name: Blank verse
techniques.definition: Unrhymed iambic pentameter, in which the sentence and the line are free to disagree.
techniques.inThisBook: Milton's sentences habitually run past the line-ending, so the verse arrives at its main verb late and the reader holds several clauses in suspense — the opening sentence takes sixteen lines to reach its imperative, 'Sing'.

techniques.name: Beginning in the middle
techniques.definition: Opening an epic after the decisive events, and supplying the earlier history later through a character's narration.
techniques.inThisBook: The war in Heaven has been over for nine days when the poem starts. Books V to VIII are Raphael filling in the past, so the exposition is a warning delivered to the two people it concerns.

techniques.name: Epic simile
techniques.definition: An extended comparison that leaves the narrative for several lines and acquires a life of its own.
techniques.inThisBook: The fallen angels lie thick as autumn leaves in Vallombrosa; Satan's shield is the moon seen through Galileo's glass. The comparisons keep reaching for the ordinary world, which is the only one the reader has.

techniques.name: Invocation
techniques.definition: A direct address to a muse or a source of inspiration, placed at the head of a book.
techniques.inThisBook: Four of them punctuate the poem, and they are where Milton speaks in his own person — most openly at the start of Book III, where the address to light becomes an account of blindness.

techniques.name: Catalogue
techniques.definition: A long list of objects or names used in place of narrative.
techniques.inThisBook: The roll-call of devils in Book I names them by the gods they will later become in Canaan, Egypt and Greece, so the list of the defeated is also a history of idolatry to come.

techniques.name: Allegory
techniques.definition: Figures who are named for what they mean, moving through a narrative alongside literal characters.
techniques.inThisBook: Sin and Death are abstractions with a family tree, and Milton lets them do physical work — keeping a gate, building a road — so that the machinery of the idea is visible in a poem otherwise committed to persons.

quotations.text: Of Man’s first disobedience, and the fruit Of that forbidden Tree, whose mortal taste Brought death into the world, and all our woe, With loss of Eden, till one greater Man Restore us, and regain the blissful seat
quotations.context: The opening of the poem, before the invocation names its muse.
quotations.analysis: The sentence withholds its verb for sixteen lines: everything here is object, and the reader is left holding disobedience, fruit, death, woe and Eden with nothing yet to do with them. Placing the remedy inside the first sentence, before the crime has been narrated, also tells you the poem is not a suspense plot.

quotations.text: That to the highth of this great argument I may assert the Eternal Providence, And justify the ways of God to men.
quotations.context: The close of the invocation to the heavenly muse.
quotations.analysis: ‘Argument’ means the poem’s subject and also a case put to a court, and Milton takes the second sense seriously enough to have God testify in Book III. ‘Justify’ is a legal verb: he is proposing to answer a charge, which is a startling thing to promise in a poem’s first thirty lines.

quotations.text: yet from those flames No light, but rather darkness visible Served only to discover sights of woe
quotations.context: Satan's first sight of Hell, as far as angels can see.
quotations.analysis: The phrase is a contradiction that works as a description: flames that illuminate nothing except how much there is to dread. Milton needs light in Hell so that the fallen can see each other and their situation, and needs it to be useless, so he invents a category of darkness that performs the office of light.

quotations.text: What though the field be lost? All is not lost; the unconquerable will, And study of revenge, immortal hate, And courage never to submit or yield:
quotations.context: Satan's first speech to Beelzebub on the burning lake.
quotations.analysis: Read the list, not the tone: an unconquerable will, a course of study in revenge, and hate described as immortal. Three of the four items are heroic virtues and one is simply a refusal to stop, and the speech works on the reader exactly as it works on the legions — by sounding like resolve before it can be inspected as a programme.

quotations.text: The mind is its own place, and in itself Can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven.
quotations.context: Satan taking possession of Hell on landing.
quotations.analysis: The claim is refuted by the speaker himself three books later, when he finds that the mind being its own place is precisely the trouble. The symmetry of the line invites agreement before the sense has been checked: it is the kind of sentence that survives detached from its speaker, which is how it usually travels.

quotations.text: Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heaven.
quotations.context: The conclusion of Satan's speech on first surveying his new kingdom.
quotations.analysis: The line presents a choice that was never on offer — nobody asked him to choose between ruling and serving — and its balance disguises the fact that one half is imaginary. It also sets the terms the rest of the poem will dismantle, since service in Heaven is shown to involve conversation, work and food, and reigning in Hell turns out to mean addressing an audience with nowhere else to go.

quotations.text: Awake, arise, or be for ever fallen!
quotations.context: Satan rousing the legions lying stunned on the lake.
quotations.analysis: Three imperatives and a threat, all in one line of monosyllables after hundreds of lines of elaborate syntax — the sudden plainness is the point. 'Fallen' does double work as a military disgrace and as their actual physical position, and the whole sentence can be shouted, which is what it is for.

quotations.text: Long is the way And hard, that out of Hell leads up to light;
quotations.speaker: Satan
quotations.context: Satan addressing the assembly before volunteering for the journey alone.
quotations.analysis: He is describing a route through Chaos and stating, without noticing, the moral condition of everyone listening. The line is also a piece of management: by making the errand sound impossible he ensures nobody else offers to share it, and the sole risk becomes sole credit.

quotations.text: The one seemed woman to the waist, and fair, But ended foul in many a scaly fold Voluminous and vast, a serpent armed With mortal sting.
quotations.context: The first description of Sin, seated at the gates of Hell.
quotations.analysis: Milton gives the allegory a joint: fair above, foul below, with the change of substance happening at the waist. The serpent's shape arrives here, long before Eden, so that when Satan enters a real snake in Book IX he is putting on something already in the family.

quotations.text: Chaos umpire sits, And by decision more embroils the fray By which he reigns; next him, high arbiter, Chance governs all.
quotations.context: The description of the abyss Satan must cross.
quotations.analysis: Both officials named here are supposed to settle disputes, and both make them worse: the umpire's rulings increase the brawl he presides over. Milton is describing a region without providence, and he does it by borrowing the vocabulary of courts and games and showing it failing.

quotations.text: Hail, holy Light, offspring of Heaven first-born!
quotations.context: The invocation opening Book III, as the poem leaves Hell for Heaven.
quotations.analysis: A blind man greets the one thing he cannot have, and the greeting is a formal salutation, not a lament. The passage that follows makes the poem’s structure into biography: he has just come up out of darkness in the story, and has not come up out of it at all.

quotations.text: I made him just and right, Sufficient to have stood, though free to fall.
quotations.speaker: God the Father
quotations.context: God, seeing Satan approach the new world, states in advance where the fault will lie.
quotations.analysis: The whole defence is balanced on one line, and on the difference between 'sufficient' and 'certain'. Had man been made unable to fall, the standing would have been mechanical; the poem's God would rather be accused of cruelty than build a creature whose obedience proves nothing.

quotations.text: Freely they stood who stood, and fell who fell.
quotations.speaker: God the Father
quotations.context: Extending the same argument from man to the angels.
quotations.analysis: Nine words, eight of them monosyllables, and the same adverb governing both halves — the freedom is identical on either side of the outcome. The chiasmus makes standing and falling grammatically equal, which is exactly the claim: nothing in the arrangement favoured one result over the other.

quotations.text: Which way I fly is Hell; myself am Hell; And, in the lowest deep, a lower deep Still threatening to devour me opens wide,
quotations.speaker: Satan
quotations.context: Alone on Mount Niphates, in sight of Eden, before entering the garden.
quotations.analysis: This is the answer to his own boast in Book I: the mind being its own place is the trap, not the escape. The geometry is the frightening part: a lowest deep that opens on a lower one means there is no floor, and Milton gives the idea in four monosyllables before the sentence stops.

quotations.text: So farewell hope, and with hope farewell fear, Farewell remorse! All good to me is lost; Evil, be thou my good:
quotations.speaker: Satan
quotations.context: The conclusion of the soliloquy on Niphates, where he considers repentance and rejects it.
quotations.analysis: He gives up fear in the same breath as hope, which is an accurate account of what despair buys. The last clause is an address, not a statement: he is conscripting evil the way a poet conscripts a muse, and the sentence has the shape of a prayer with the object swapped.

quotations.text: For contemplation he and valour formed, For softness she and sweet attractive grace; He for God only, she for God in him.
quotations.context: The narrator's first description of Adam and Eve, seen through Satan's eyes.
quotations.analysis: The doctrine is stated in the most memorable line available, with the parallel structure doing the work of proof. Notice who is looking: the description is placed inside Satan’s view, and the poem’s own drama spends five more books declining to behave as the line prescribes.

quotations.text: My author and disposer, what thou bidd’st Unargued I obey; so God ordains: God is thy law, thou mine: to know no more Is woman’s happiest knowledge, and her praise.
quotations.speaker: Eve
quotations.context: Eve answering Adam at the end of their first day in the poem.
quotations.analysis: She states the hierarchy more absolutely than Adam ever does, and she states it in an argument — the speech is fluent, ordered and rhetorically confident, which is not what unargued obedience sounds like. Five books later she will open a debate on exactly this question and win it.

quotations.text: With thee conversing I forget all time, All seasons and their change: all please alike.
quotations.speaker: Eve
quotations.context: Eve to Adam in the garden at evening.
quotations.analysis: The love poem she then speaks is built as a list of everything she likes and a repeat of the same list with the word 'without' inserted, so that the structure itself performs the point. Here at its head, 'conversing' carries its older sense of living with as well as talking to, and it is talk that the Fall will first spoil.

quotations.text: Abashed the Devil stood, And felt how awful goodness is, and saw Virtue in her shape how lovely
quotations.context: Satan, discovered in the garden, faced down by the young angel Zephon.
quotations.analysis: The verb comes first and the subject second, so the shame arrives before the person it belongs to. ‘Awful’ still means awe-inspiring here, and the moment matters because it is the one place where Satan is shown finding good attractive, and then walking on.

quotations.text: So spake the Seraph Abdiel, faithful found; Among the faithless, faithful only he;
quotations.context: After Abdiel has answered Satan's argument in front of the assembled rebel host.
quotations.analysis: The repetition works like a count: faithful, faithless, faithful, with the tally narrowing to 'only he'. Milton, writing after the Restoration had made his own politics unspeakable, gives his invented character the one action available to a defeated dissenter — to say so out loud and then leave.

quotations.text: ‘Let there be light!’ said God; and forthwith light Ethereal, first of things, quintessence pure, Sprung from the Deep
quotations.speaker: Raphael
quotations.context: Raphael's account of the first day of creation.
quotations.analysis: The quoted command takes half a line and the consequence begins in the same line, so the syntax enacts the speed of the thing described. Milton then cannot leave it alone and spends three clauses classifying the light, which is the characteristic movement of this book: a scriptural sentence followed by a poet unable to stop looking at it.

quotations.text: Heaven is for thee too high To know what passes there; be lowly wise; Think only what concerns thee and thy being;
quotations.speaker: Raphael
quotations.context: Raphael closing down Adam's questions about the motion of the heavens.
quotations.analysis: ‘Lowly wise’ means wise about the right things, not ignorant, and the proof is that the angel has just spent three books answering questions. The serpent will offer Adam's wife the exact opposite bargain — knowledge as promotion — and the phrasing of this warning is what makes the offer recognisable.

quotations.text: And what is faith, love, virtue, unassayed Alone, without exterior help sustained?
quotations.speaker: Eve
quotations.context: Eve arguing that she and Adam should work in separate parts of the garden.
quotations.analysis: This is Milton's own position, put in the mouth of the character about to be ruined by acting on it: he had argued in print that a virtue never exposed to its opposite is worth nothing. The poem does not refute her. It simply lets the argument be correct and the morning be a disaster.

quotations.text: Go; for thy stay, not free, absents thee more; Go in thy native innocence, rely On what thou hast of virtue, summon all; For God towards thee hath done his part; do thine.
quotations.speaker: Adam
quotations.context: Adam conceding the argument and letting Eve go alone.
quotations.analysis: He gives way on the same principle he is worried about: keeping her by command would make her presence worthless. The last four words are the whole theology of the poem compressed into a domestic exchange, and they are said by a man who has just lost an argument he was right to be having.

quotations.text: So saying, her rash hand in evil hour Forth reaching to the fruit, she plucked, she eat. Earth felt the wound, and Nature from her seat, Sighing through all her works, gave signs of woe
quotations.context: The Fall itself, at the end of the serpent's argument.
quotations.analysis: Two monosyllabic verbs, side by side without a conjunction, take up less room than the adjective attached to her hand — the act is smaller than everything around it. Then the sentence widens instantly to the whole planet, and the disproportion between the gesture and the consequence is the effect Milton has been building for nine books.

quotations.text: he scrupled not to eat, Against his better knowledge, not deceived, But fondly overcome with female charm.
quotations.context: Adam eating the fruit Eve brings him.
quotations.analysis: The clauses are arranged to remove every excuse in turn: not ignorant, not tricked, simply unwilling to be left. 'Fondly' means foolishly, and the line is the poem's coldest, because it denies Adam the dignity of a mistake and gives him a motive most readers recognise.

quotations.text: Nor love thy life, nor hate; but what thou livest Live well; how long or short, permit to Heaven.
quotations.speaker: Michael
quotations.context: Michael answering Adam, after the vision of the lazar-house of diseases.
quotations.analysis: Adam has just asked how to meet death and been shown every way it arrives. The answer rejects both obvious postures, clinging and despair, and puts the weight on an adverb: what matters is the manner of the life, not its length, the first piece of advice in the poem that applies to a reader.

quotations.text: then wilt thou not be loth To leave this Paradise, but shalt possess A Paradise within thee, happier far.
quotations.speaker: Michael
quotations.context: Michael's summary of what Adam is to add to his knowledge before leaving.
quotations.analysis: The offer is comparative — happier far — which is a startling thing to say to a man being evicted from the best place there has ever been. The list that leads up to it is all practice: faith, virtue, patience, temperance, love. Paradise becomes something done, not somewhere lived.

quotations.text: The world was all before them, where to choose Their place of rest, and Providence their guide. They, hand in hand, with wandering steps and slow, Through Eden took their solitary way.
quotations.context: The last four lines of the poem.
quotations.analysis: Every phrase pulls two ways: a whole world to choose from and nowhere in particular to go; guided, and wandering; hand in hand, and solitary. Milton refuses either a triumph or a lament, and the final rhythm — slow, with a caesura in each of the last two lines — makes the reader walk out at their pace.

timeline.label: John Milton born in Bread Street, London
timeline.detail: The son of a scrivener and composer, in a household that could afford tutors and music.

timeline.label: Milton travels in Italy
timeline.detail: He later wrote of having visited the aged Galileo, then a prisoner of the Inquisition; Galileo's telescope appears in the poem.

timeline.label: Areopagitica published
timeline.detail: His argument against pre-publication licensing turns on the claim that a virtue never tested is no virtue — the position Eve takes in Book IX.

timeline.label: Charles I executed; Milton defends the regicide in print
timeline.detail: The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates appears within weeks, and Milton is appointed Secretary for Foreign Tongues to the Council of State.

timeline.label: Milton is completely blind
timeline.detail: From this point everything he writes is dictated, including the whole of the epic.

timeline.label: The Restoration
timeline.detail: Milton goes into hiding, is arrested and released; his defences of the regicide are burnt by the hangman.

timeline.label: Plague drives Milton out of London
timeline.detail: He took a cottage at Chalfont St Giles in Buckinghamshire, where work on the poem continued.

timeline.label: Paradise Lost published in ten books
timeline.detail: Printed in London the year after the Great Fire, with a contract paying Milton five pounds down.

timeline.label: Paradise Regained and Samson Agonistes published together
timeline.detail: The brief epic of the temptation in the wilderness, and a tragedy about a blind man among his enemies.

timeline.label: The twelve-book second edition; Milton dies
timeline.detail: Books VII and X were each split in two and a few lines added. Milton died in November and was buried at St Giles-without-Cripplegate.

timeline.label: Tonson's illustrated folio
timeline.detail: The first grand edition, published by subscription, which made the poem a national monument.

timeline.label: Blake begins The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
timeline.detail: The first of the Romantic readings that take Milton's Satan as the poem's real energy — a reading the poem's structure was built to resist.

places.name: Mount Sinai
places.note: Oreb, or of Sinai: the mountain named in the opening invocation as where the shepherd Moses was first inspired.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Zion hill and Siloa's brook, offered in the invocation as the alternative source of the poet's inspiration.

places.name: Mount Helicon

criticalViews.position: The Romantic reading: Satan as the poem's true energy
criticalViews.summary: From the 1790s onwards, readers have argued that Milton writes at full power in Hell and at half power in Heaven, and that the sympathy the poem generates for its rebel is not fully under its author's control.
criticalViews.counter: It requires ignoring the poem's shape. Satan's speeches get shorter and his form smaller as the work proceeds, and Books XI and XII belong to somebody else entirely.

criticalViews.position: The theological reading: a poem about free will
criticalViews.summary: On this account the epic is doing exactly what it says in line twenty-six — mounting a defence of divine justice by insisting that creatures who could not have failed would prove nothing, and that the Fall therefore belongs to the people who chose it.
criticalViews.counter: A defence conducted by the defendant, in speeches many readers find chilly, may win the argument and lose the case.

criticalViews.position: The political reading: a defeated republican writing after the Restoration
criticalViews.summary: Milton wrote for a revolution, served its government, and finished the poem under the monarchy it had killed. Read this way, the questions of who deserves to rule, what service means and how a lone dissenter behaves are not decoration.
criticalViews.counter: The parallels do not line up neatly: the poem’s rebel against a monarch is Satan, which wrecks any simple mapping of Milton’s politics onto the plot.

criticalViews.summary: Criticism since the 1970s has examined the gap between the hierarchy the poem asserts and the initiative it repeatedly gives to Eve — the strongest argument in Book IX is hers, and so is the first step towards reconciliation in Book X.
criticalViews.counter: The poem also gives her the fall, and states her subordination in its own narrating voice, not only through a character.

essayQuestions.question: Does Paradise Lost succeed in justifying the ways of God to men?
essayQuestions.focus: Free will, foreknowledge and the poem's stated purpose
plan: Take the promise literally: 'justify' is a legal verb, so establish what charge is being answered.
Set out God's own defence in Book III — created sufficient to have stood, though free to fall — and note that it is put as argument, not assertion.
Test it on the angels, where Abdiel in Book V shows that the rebellion was refusable by somebody standing in the same room.
Turn to Book IX, where the doctrine becomes a domestic argument and Adam concedes on exactly the principle God has stated.
Weigh the cost: a case won in Book III may still be lost in tone, and decide whether Books XI and XII repair that or confirm it.

essayQuestions.question: How far is Satan the hero of Paradise Lost?
essayQuestions.focus: Rhetoric, structure and the reader's sympathy
plan: Begin with what the speeches actually promise: unconquerable will, a study of revenge, and a reign that nobody offered as an alternative to service.
Trace the diminishing shape — soliloquy on Niphates in Book IV, the toad and the mist, the serpent in Book IX, the hissing in Book X.
Distinguish the reader's experience of the verse from the poem's judgement, and consider whether Milton means the seduction to happen to us.
Use Abdiel as the control: a character given the same information who does the opposite.
Conclude on structure — the last two books remove Satan entirely, which is an argument in itself.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss Milton's presentation of Eve.
essayQuestions.focus: Hierarchy, argument and the poem's internal contradictions
plan: Start with the narrator's own statement of hierarchy in Book IV and note who is looking when it is made.
Read her speech of obedience as a rhetorical performance, fluent and shapely, and ask what that does to the word 'unargued'.
Give full weight to the separation scene: the argument about untested virtue is Milton's own published position.
Follow the aftermath in Book X, where she proposes reconciliation and Adam is still assigning blame.
Decide whether the poem contains a contradiction or dramatises one deliberately.

essayQuestions.question: What does the ending of Paradise Lost offer its readers?
essayQuestions.focus: Exile, consolation and the last four lines
plan: Establish what Michael has actually shown Adam in Books XI and XII, and how the method changes from vision to narration.
Examine the paradise within: a comparative claim, happier far, made to somebody being evicted.
Read the closing lines phrase by phrase, noting how each carries its own contradiction.
Set the ending against Book I, where exile produced rage, and measure the distance travelled.
Consider what a reader in 1667 London — plague, fire, a restored monarchy — would hear in a consolation of this kind.

discussionQuestions: Satan's finest speeches are in the first two books and he never sounds that way again. Is the decline a judgement, or a loss of interest?
Eve argues that virtue untested is not virtue. Does the poem ever answer her, or only show the consequences?
Adam is explicitly not deceived. Does that make his fall worse than hers, or more forgivable?
Raphael tells Adam to be lowly wise after answering questions for three books. Where is the line meant to fall?
The poem ends with the whole world available and two people walking slowly. Is that a consolation or a sentence?

related.why: The epic Milton measured himself against most closely, down to the arming, the councils and the visit to the underworld.
The war poem behind the war in Heaven, and the source of the catalogue and the extended simile.

Shelley takes her epigraph from Book X, and her creature reads Paradise Lost and identifies with both Adam and Satan.
